title: The Reflected Face: How the Call Descends and the Answer Rises by the Mystery of Correspondence
arc: Beginning from the simple observation that a man bending over water sees his own face cast downward with the head reversed, the teaching unfolds the cosmic mystery of correspondence: this inverted reflection is the sign of the Call sent from above into the depths and of the Answer rising from the depths back to the First Man, and the shadow cast on the earth is the sign that the body has been lifted up out of the Deep.
reading:
This chapter takes one of the most ordinary facts of nature — that when a person stoops over water and looks down, he sees his own face below him with the head reversed and the feet seemingly above — and reads it as a complete diagram of the work of redemption. The teaching is not really about water and reflection at all; it is about how the upper realm imprints itself in the lower, and how what is below answers back to what is above. The whole cosmos, the master says, is full of mysteries, and this is one of them: that nothing in the natural world is bare nature, every appearance is a sign of a spiritual operation.

The opening movement fixes the image. The man of heaven stands at a water and gazes downward; his face appears in the water turned the wrong way up, head pointing down, feet pointing above. This is read as the mystery of the Call cast down by the First Man into the cosmos of Darkness. The Father of Greatness sends his face into the depths as the First Man, but in that descent the image is, as it were, inverted: what is highest in the source must become lowest in its reception, the head must come down to where the feet should be, in order to keep watch over the captive light below. The reflected face in water is therefore the natural figure of accommodation — the divine truth taking the form of the lower in order to be present to the lower.

The teaching then turns the image around. The man who lifts himself up out of the water — and his face is then seen righted, no longer cast down — is the mystery of the Answer, the Hearing, which comes up from below to above, from the captive cosmos back to the First Man, the Father, and to the Living Spirit's projection. So the same reflective surface holds both motions: the descending Call when the gaze goes down, the ascending Answer when the body rises up. This is the spiritual mystery of which the chapter speaks plainly: pneumatic, not merely natural — the whole circuit of redemption read off from one act of bending and rising at a pool.

The teaching then expands the figure outward to the whole cosmos. Not only the face of a man, but the likeness of trees and the faces of cattle appear in water in the same downward-turned way; and on a vaster scale, the stars and the signs of the zodiac are reflected in the great sea. All natural things — men, animals, perceptions (trees) — hang from the stars and zodiac-signs and are begotten from them, just as the reflection hangs from its original. This is the ancient correspondence-doctrine spoken cosmologically: the heavens are the originals, the earth and sea are their mirror, every creature here is a reflected and inverted likeness of a higher truth there. The Fathers spread out from the upper place show themselves below in this same mode — their mystery becomes manifest in the lower as an icon turned downward into the place where the gaze falls.

A further figure is added: the child begotten, who as he is brought forth has the mother's shadow coming with him, hanging behind him at the moment of birth. The teaching reads this as another instance of the same law — that whatever is brought forth into ultimates carries with it the trailing image of what generated it. Begetting in the natural is a hanging-down of the heavenly state into time.

The closing movement turns the image one last time, from reflection in water to shadow on earth. Wherever a man walks, his shadow is cast upon the ground; when he rises up, the shadow extends along the earth, but its source stands upright toward heaven. This shadow is read as a great sign: it signifies that the whole body has come up out of the earth, has come up out of the Deep. That is, the very fact that the body now stands and casts a shadow downward witnesses to the prior redemption — light has been raised from the hells, the Living Soul has been brought up from where it was sunk, and what is now seen as a trailing shadow is only the after-trace of an accomplished ascent. The shadow stretched down along the ground while its substance is hanging upward is the signature of regeneration: the lowest still bears the mark of the depth, but the substance itself is already above.

Read as one arc, the chapter teaches three coordinated truths under one image. First, the inverted reflection in water is the Call — Divine Truth coming down into the realm of self-love, accommodating itself by inversion so that its head is set among the depths to seek what is lost. Second, the rising of the man from the water is the Answer — the soul's response, the Hearing, returning upward to the First Man and the Father. Third, the shadow on the earth is the after-sign of redemption — proof that the body has been raised out of the Deep, with the natural still bearing a trace of darkness but the substance now standing erect toward heaven. The whole created order, then, is a vast water and a vast ground in which the heavenly originals are continuously reflected and continuously casting shadows; reading these signs rightly is itself part of the chosen one's work, for the cosmos stands fast in mystery and is full of mysteries everywhere a man knows how to look.
